newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvians fear bloodbath as president talks tough.
newsitem.headline: Peruvians fear bloodbath as president talks tough.

text.p: Fearing a bloodbath, ordinary Peruvians worried on Sunday that their tough-talking president may have gone too far in denouncing hostage takers as terrorists and not offering them a clear way out.
"No one is in agreement with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Front (MRTA), but it's plainly stupid to speak to them the way President (Alberto) Fujimori did," said taxi-driver Francisco Sanchez.
"It's just not realistic, it's a dangerous attitude. Talking like that is the surest way to make this end tragically -- with plenty of blood."

In his first spoken remarks since the MRTA stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima last Tuesday, Fujimori scorned the Marxist guerrilla movement as "uncivilized ... sowing death and destruction."
He scorned them for "attempting a dialogue while placing an AKM (semi-automatic) rifle on the neck of hostages."
And he labeled MRTA prisoners, whose freedom is the hostage-takers' principal demand, as "the perpetrators of murder and terrorist attacks."
On the streets of Lima, nervous Peruvians predicted violence unless the president toned down his public stance.

"Who knows what he's saying to them behind the scenes, but he went too far last night. He has to stay calm. It's ridiculous to tell a desperate group like that to put down their arms, release all their hostages and then start working out a solution," said newspaper-seller Abraham Garcia.

"Fujimori should be proposing practical solutions to this crisis, not playing the hard man. If you ask me, they should let the rebels go back to the jungle, perhaps with five of their top hostages as security and a few -- just a few -- of the prisoners they are asking for."

Entering a church on Sunday close to the Japanese ambassador's residence in the middle-class district of San Isidro, housewife Maria Benavides said she would pray for both Fujimori and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.

"Fujimori is on a knife-edge. All his hard-won successes are at stake. And Cerpa Cartolini is playing his last card -- he'll either end a martyr or turn the MRTA into a new power. I ask God to soften both their hearts and bring them together."

While Fujimori's speech followed the tough line he has always taken against guerrillas which has been popular in the past, citizens are more sceptical now that the president's credibility has been badly hurt by the surprise attack.
"His popularity was falling anyway with all the unemployment and poverty here, and I don't think what he said last night showed him in a good light," said newspaper seller Manuel Caldani.

"What he has to realise is that the MRTA action is in a way a big response, or at least a reflection of the great suffering of the people of Peru. The MRTA members are ordinary people trying to speak up for the poor. Fujimori should be a little bit more careful and respectful."

The crisis could not have come at a worse time for Fujimori, whose traditionally high levels of popularity had plummeted to a five-year low of around 45 percent as poverty remained entrenched and the economy stagnated.
Outside the ambassador's residence, one of the 900 police officers on guard described his president's stance as "radical, adventurous, and typically hard ... but extremely dangerous."
Tapping an automatic rifle, he nodded nervously toward the building where several hundred yards (metres) away about 20 heavily-armed MRTA guerrillas held 340 hostages.
"If you ask me, I think we'll be going in. And if we go in, expect deaths."
Across the nation Sunday, Peruvians hoisted flags in a show of solidarity with the hostages and tried to carry on with life as normal.
In San Isidro, street hawkers peddled their wares while residents did their weekend shopping.

"Life can't stop because of this. Not for us anyway," said fruit-seller Manuel Serrano from the Lima slum of Villa Salvador, a former stronghold of Peru's better-known guerrilla movement Shining Path.
"In the past, the terrorists massacred the little people, and no-one took any notice. Now, they've got all the rich people in there, but the rest of us aren't really affected in a practical way."
